conflicts/yugoslav-wars/name: The Yugoslav wars, Bosnia and Srebrenica
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/religionRoleNote: The wars that destroyed Yugoslavia were driven by nationalist politicians, the collapse of communism and competing territorial projects. Because Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks speak essentially the same language, religion — Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim — was the main marker of national identity, and war aims of ‘ethnic cleansing’ were in practice religious cleansing: mosques, churches and monasteries were systematically destroyed and victims identified by their names and faith. Michael Sells argues that religious mythology, especially the Serbian Kosovo myth, was central to genocidal ideology (‘Christoslavism’); Vjekoslav Perica shows how churches became ‘national churches’ that sacralised nationalism; others, such as Laura Silber and Allan Little, emphasise political leaders who used religion instrumentally while being themselves ex-communists. The term ‘pretext’ fits the leaders; ‘contributing’ better fits the role of religious identity and clergy.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/sides/0/name: Serbian forces (Yugoslav People’s Army, Army of Republika Srpska, Croatian Serb forces, paramilitaries such as Arkan’s Tigers and the Scorpions)
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/sides/1/name: Croatian forces (Croatian Army, Croatian Defence Council in Bosnia)
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/sides/2/name: Bosnian government and Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/sides/2/faith: Mainly Bosniak Muslim, with Serb and Croat members, especially in Sarajevo and Tuzla
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/sides/3/name: International actors (UN Protection Force, NATO, European and US mediators)
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/summary: As Yugoslavia disintegrated in 1991, wars in Slovenia, Croatia and then Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992–95) pitted Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks against one another in campaigns of ‘ethnic cleansing’ that targeted religious identity, culminating in the genocide of some 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995. Churches and religious leaders were drawn into national causes, sometimes blessing fighters, while others pleaded for peace. The Dayton Agreement of November 1995 ended the Bosnian war.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/story:
Yugoslavia contained Orthodox Serbs, Montenegrins and Macedonians, Catholic Croats and Slovenes, and Muslim Bosniaks and Albanians. The Second World War had left terrible memories: the Croatian Ustaša state, tolerated and in part supported by Catholic clergy, murdered hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma, notably at Jasenovac, and forcibly converted Serbs to Catholicism; Serbian Četniks massacred Muslims and Croats. Tito’s communist regime suppressed these memories under ‘brotherhood and unity’. After Tito’s death in 1980 and amid economic crisis, nationalists revived them. The Serbian Orthodox Church’s Kosovo myth — Prince Lazar’s choice of a heavenly kingdom at the battle of Kosovo in 1389 — was invoked as Lazar’s relics toured Serb lands in 1988–89, and on the 600th anniversary, 28 June 1989, Slobodan Milošević addressed a huge crowd at Gazimestan, warning that battles might again be fought.

In 1990 multi-party elections brought nationalists to power in the republics. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. After a ten-day war Slovenia was allowed to go, but in Croatia rebel Serbs, backed by the Yugoslav People’s Army, seized about a third of the country. Vukovar was besieged for three months and destroyed; after its fall on 18 November 1991 some 200 wounded and hospital staff were taken to the Ovčara farm and murdered. Dubrovnik was shelled. Croatian forces also expelled and killed Serb civilians, and the United Nations deployed peacekeepers in 1992.

Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most mixed republic, declared independence after a referendum boycotted by Serbs in early 1992. From April Bosnian Serb forces under Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić, with Serbian paramilitaries, seized some 70 per cent of the territory and ‘cleansed’ it of non-Serbs: towns such as Bijeljina, Zvornik, Foča, Višegrad and Prijedor saw mass killings, detention camps such as Omarska and Keraterm, and systematic rape. Mosques, Catholic churches and Ottoman monuments were deliberately destroyed, including the sixteenth-century Ferhadija mosque in Banja Luka in May 1993; the National Library in Sarajevo was burned in August 1992. Sarajevo endured a siege from April 1992 to February 1996, in which over 11,000 people died, including the shelling of the Markale market in 1994 and 1995.

In 1993 a second war broke out between Bosnian Croats, backed by Tuđman’s Croatia, and the Bosniak-led government. Croat forces massacred Muslim villagers at Ahmići in April 1993 and destroyed Mostar’s Ottoman Old Bridge in November; the government army, joined by some foreign mujahideen, also committed abuses against Croat and Serb civilians. The Washington Agreement of March 1994 ended the Croat–Bosniak war. Meanwhile, UN ‘safe areas’ such as Srebrenica, Žepa and Goražde were left lightly defended.

In July 1995 Mladić’s forces overran Srebrenica. Dutch UN peacekeepers could not protect the population; women and children were bussed out, while around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were captured and executed over a few days and buried in mass graves, many later moved to conceal them. Video later showed an Orthodox priest blessing members of the Scorpions unit before they shot six prisoners. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and the International Court of Justice later ruled the massacre genocide. In August 1995 Croatia’s Operation Storm retook the Krajina, causing some 150,000–200,000 Serbs to flee, with hundreds of civilians killed; NATO air strikes after the second Markale massacre and a Croat–Bosniak offensive brought the Serbs to the table.

The Dayton Agreement, negotiated in Ohio under Richard Holbrooke and signed in Paris on 14 December 1995, kept Bosnia as one state divided into a Bosniak–Croat Federation and Republika Srpska under a complex ethnic power-sharing system and international oversight. Karadžić and Mladić were later convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity at The Hague; Milošević died in 2006 during his trial. Conflict moved to Kosovo in 1998–99, ending after NATO’s bombing of Serbia, and to Macedonia in 2001.

The religious communities emerged as guardians of national identity in the new states. The Serbian Orthodox Church canonised some wartime figures and many of its hierarchs defended Karadžić; the Greek Orthodox Church even honoured him in 1993. The Catholic Church in Croatia, led by Cardinal Franjo Kuharić, called for respect for all victims but closely associated itself with the Croatian state. Islamic institutions became more central to Bosniak identity. At the same time interreligious councils, Franciscan friars of Bosnia, and individual Orthodox, Catholic and Muslim leaders worked for reconciliation, a task still unfinished in divided towns and contested memorials.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/nameOfGod: Serbian nationalists drew on the Kosovo covenant of Prince Lazar, the three-fingered Orthodox salute and the slogan ‘Only Unity Saves the Serbs’ (Samo sloga Srbina spasava) under the Orthodox cross; Orthodox priests blessed some units and paramilitaries, and Karadžić presented his cause as defending Christian Europe against an Islamic state. Croatian nationalism used the Catholic rosary, the cult of Cardinal Alojzije Stepinac and Our Lady of Medjugorje as identity symbols, and Croat units in Herzegovina bore Catholic insignia. Some Bosniak units adopted Islamic names and slogans, and foreign mujahideen fought as jihadists. Religious buildings of the enemy were targeted precisely because they signified the presence of the other people.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/religiousCauses/: Religion was the chief marker distinguishing Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks, who share a language, so national struggles became religious in form.
The Serbian Orthodox Kosovo myth and its revival around the 1989 anniversary sacralised Serbian nationalism and portrayed Muslims as betrayers of Christ.
Unresolved memories of the Second World War, including Ustaša forced conversions and massacres of Orthodox Serbs, and Četnik massacres of Muslims, fed mutual fear.
Churches that had suffered under communism embraced nationalist movements as partners in religious revival after 1989.
Propaganda portrayed Bosniaks as Islamic fundamentalists seeking a jihad state, and Croats and Serbs as crusaders, intensifying religious polarisation.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/otherCauses/0: The economic crisis and debt of 1980s Yugoslavia and the end of communist legitimacy after 1989.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/otherCauses/1: Ex-communist leaders, notably Milošević and Tuđman, used nationalism to win and keep power.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/otherCauses/2: Competing territorial projects for a Greater Serbia and a Greater Croatia, including the 1991 Karađorđevo talks on partitioning Bosnia.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/otherCauses/3: The Serb-dominated Yugoslav army’s control of weapons, and the arms embargo that disadvantaged the Bosnian government.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/otherCauses/4: International hesitation and divided diplomacy that rewarded military faits accomplis.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/triggers/0: The declarations of independence of Slovenia and Croatia on 25 June 1991.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/triggers/1: The Bosnian independence referendum of February–March 1992 and international recognition in April 1992.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/triggers/2: The Serb seizure of territory and siege of Sarajevo in April 1992.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/0/text: Milošević addresses the 600th anniversary of the battle of Kosovo at Gazimestan (28 June).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/1/text: Slovenia and Croatia declare independence (25 June); ten-day war in Slovenia; war in Croatia; fall of Vukovar and Ovčara massacre (November).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/2/text: Bosnia declares independence; war begins in April; siege of Sarajevo; camps at Omarska and Keraterm; burning of Sarajevo’s National Library (August).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/3/text: Croat–Bosniak war; Ahmići massacre (April); Ferhadija mosque destroyed (May); Stari Most in Mostar destroyed (November); ICTY established.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/4/text: Markale market massacre (February); Washington Agreement ends the Croat–Bosniak war (March).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/5/text: Srebrenica genocide (July); Operation Storm (August); NATO Operation Deliberate Force; Dayton Agreement (November–December).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/6/text: Pope John Paul II visits Sarajevo (April).
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/7/text: War in Kosovo ends after NATO bombing of Serbia.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/8/text: ICTY Appeals Chamber confirms the Srebrenica massacre as genocide in the Krstić case.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/9/text: International Court of Justice rules Srebrenica genocide and finds Serbia failed to prevent it.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/timeline/10/text: Final appeal confirms Ratko Mladić’s life sentence for genocide.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/0/role: President of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/0/focu: Used Serbian nationalism and the Kosovo myth to rise to power and backed Serb forces in Croatia and Bosnia.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/0/outc: Extradited to The Hague in 2001; died in 2006 before his trial ended.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/1/focu: Led Croatia to independence, sponsored the Bosnian Croat statelet of Herceg-Bosna and ordered Operation Storm.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/1/outc: Died in office in 1999; ICTY judgments later named him in a joint criminal enterprise in Bosnia.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/2/focu: Led the Bosnian government through the war and signed Dayton; his earlier Islamic Declaration was used by opponents to portray him as a fundamentalist.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/3/focu: Directed the Bosnian Serb political leadership responsible for ethnic cleansing and the siege of Sarajevo, presenting himself as a defender of Orthodox Christianity.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/3/outc: Arrested in 2008; convicted of genocide at Srebrenica and sentenced to life imprisonment.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/4/role: Commander of the Army of Republika Srpska
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/4/focu: Commanded the siege of Sarajevo and the capture of Srebrenica.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/4/outc: Arrested in 2011; convicted of genocide and sentenced to life imprisonment in 2017, upheld in 2021.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/5/role: Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church 1990–2009
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/5/focu: Defended Serb national claims but appealed repeatedly for peace and condemned crimes, saying that if a Greater Serbia could only be gained by crime he would not accept it.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/5/outc: Revered for personal asceticism; criticised for the church’s ties to Bosnian Serb leaders.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/6/role: Catholic Archbishop of Sarajevo, cardinal from 1994
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/6/focu: Remained in besieged Sarajevo and spoke for a united, multi-religious Bosnia.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/6/outc: Hosted John Paul II’s visit in 1997 and led the Catholic Church in Bosnia until 2022.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/keyPeople/7/focu: Supported Croatian independence while urging Croats not to take revenge and to respect enemies’ lives and property.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/casualties/note: For Bosnia and Herzegovina the Research and Documentation Centre in Sarajevo (Bosnian Book of the Dead) identified about 97,000–100,000 killed, of whom roughly 40 per cent were civilians and most were Bosniaks; the ICTY demographic unit reached a similar figure. Deaths in the war in Croatia are estimated at about 20,000. Srebrenica alone accounted for some 8,000 victims. The range covers Slovenia, Croatia and Bosnia in 1991–95; the Kosovo war of 1998–99 added about 13,000 further deaths. Over four million people were displaced.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/effects/0: Yugoslavia was replaced by independent states, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided by Dayton into two ethnically defined entities under international supervision.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/effects/1: Ethnic cleansing largely succeeded: most towns became overwhelmingly mono-ethnic, and many refugees never returned.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/effects/2: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (1993–2017) became a landmark of international criminal law, convicting leaders of all sides.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/effects/3: International failure at Srebrenica shaped the later doctrine of the ‘responsibility to protect’.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/effectsOnChurch/: The Serbian Orthodox and Croatian Catholic churches emerged as national institutions closely tied to their states, criticised for failing to confront crimes committed in their nations’ name.
Thousands of mosques, hundreds of Catholic churches and many Orthodox churches and monasteries were destroyed; their rebuilding, such as the Ferhadija mosque in 2016, became a test of reconciliation.
Interreligious councils, including the Inter-religious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1997), were founded with Orthodox, Catholic, Muslim and Jewish leaders.
The Franciscans of Bosna Srebrena, who stayed with their communities and opposed partition, became an example of Catholic resistance to ethnic nationalism.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/legacy: The Bosnian war became the paradigm of ‘ethno-religious’ conflict in post-Cold War Europe and the occasion for Europe’s first genocide since the Holocaust. It raises hard questions for churches about the fusion of faith and nation, and about how clergy who blessed fighters or canonised nationalist heroes can contribute to truth and reconciliation.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/0/tex: He repeatedly condemned ethnic cleansing, tried to visit besieged Sarajevo in 1994 and went there in April 1997, calling for forgiveness and reconciliation among all communities.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/1/tex: Despite his church’s nationalism, he declared that crimes committed in the name of the Serbian people could not be justified and that he would rather Serbia disappear than be built on crime.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/2/tex: Friars led by Fra Petar Anđelović and Fra Ivo Marković refused to support ethnic partition, stayed in mixed towns and later founded the interreligious choir Pontanima.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/3/nam: Bishop Artemije of Raška and Prizren
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/3/tex: The Serbian Orthodox bishop of Kosovo openly opposed Milošević’s policies and condemned violence against both Albanians and Serbs.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/dissenters/4/tex: He stayed in besieged Sarajevo, rejected the division of Bosnia into ethnic statelets and called on Catholics to protect their neighbours.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/campaigns/0/titl: The column from Srebrenica to Tuzla
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/campaigns/0/peop: Some 10,000–15,000 Bosniak men and boys attempting to escape through the woods
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/campaigns/0/text: On the night of 11–12 July 1995 a column of men set out across Serb-held territory towards government lines; it was ambushed and shelled near Kamenica and the Konjević Polje–Nova Kasaba road, where thousands were captured and later executed. Survivors broke through at Baljkovica on 16 July and reached Tuzla. The route is retraced each year by the Marš mira peace march.
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/campaigns/1/peop: Croatian Army under Generals Ante Gotovina and others
conflicts/yugoslav-wars/campaigns/1/text: On 4–7 August 1995 Croatian forces overran the self-declared Republic of Serbian Krajina, taking its capital Knin on 5 August. Most of the Serb population fled into Bosnia and Serbia, and the following weeks saw killings of elderly Serb civilians and widespread burning of homes.
